questions.question: [Scenario 1] [Scrum Theory & Empiricism] An enterprise product organization assigns three separate Product Owners to a single Scrum Team, with each Product Owner directing different feature sets. The team experiences conflicting priorities and missed Sprint Goals. How should the Scrum Master coach the organization? (Context variation 1.1)

options.text: Instruct the Scrum Master to act as the head Product Owner to resolve conflicts.
Enforce the Scrum Guide principle: there is only ONE Product Owner per Scrum Team to ensure single-point accountability.
Create three sub-teams within the Scrum Team, each led by one Product Owner.
Rotate the Product Owner accountability among the Developers on a Sprint-by-Sprint basis.

questions.explanation: The Scrum Guide explicitly states that the Product Owner is ONE person, not a committee. Having multiple Product Owners creates conflicting priorities and destroys accountability.

recommendation.topic: Empirical Process Control (Transparency, Inspection, Adaptation)
recommendation.linkText: Read Knowledge Hub: Empirical Process Control & Complexity
recommendation.action: Review how Scrum manages risk in complex environments compared to predictive waterfall planning.

questions.question: [Scenario 2] [Scrum Values & Culture] During Sprint Execution, a key stakeholder requests a critical bug fix that is completely unrelated to the current Sprint Goal. The Product Owner wants to add it immediately. What is the most appropriate action by the Developers and Product Owner? (Context variation 1.2)

options.text: The Developers must automatically accept all mid-Sprint additions requested by the Product Owner.
The Sprint must be cancelled immediately whenever new work is identified.
Scope can be negotiated between Product Owner and Developers as long as the change does not endanger the Sprint Goal or compromise quality.
Developers should secretly fix the bug without informing the Product Owner or documenting it in the Sprint Backlog.

questions.explanation: In Scrum, scope may be clarified and re-negotiated between the Product Owner and Developers as more is learned, provided the change does not endanger the Sprint Goal.

recommendation.topic: Scrum Values (Commitment, Courage, Focus, Openness, Respect)
recommendation.action: Evaluate your team's psychological safety and servant leadership stance across 7 maturity dimensions.

questions.question: [Scenario 3] [Scrum Team Accountabilities] A Scrum Team completes all user stories in a Sprint, but due to time pressure, they skipped regression testing and integration documentation. The Product Owner wants to release the code to production. What should happen? (Context variation 1.3)

options.text: Release the code, because Product Owner approval overrides the Definition of Done.
Items that do not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released or presented as part of an Increment; they return to the Product Backlog.
Mark the items as 90% Done and carry the remaining testing effort into a 'Testing Sprint'.
Change the Definition of Done retroactively to exclude regression testing.

questions.explanation: If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review. It returns to the Product Backlog for future refinement.

recommendation.topic: Scrum Team Accountabilities (PO, SM, Developers)
recommendation.action: Re-align on self-management, cross-functionality, and boundary accountabilities without sub-teams.

questions.question: [Scenario 4] [Scrum Events & Timeboxes] An engineering committee requests that a Scrum Team halt feature development for 4 Sprints to produce a complete 500-page enterprise software architecture document. How does this align with Scrum's empirical approach? (Context variation 1.4)

options.text: It aligns perfectly, as Scrum mandates exhaustive upfront architectural blueprints before building Increments.
It contradicts empiricism; architecture in Scrum evolves organically through incremental building, inspection, and feedback on working software.
Scrum Teams should never document software under any circumstances.
The Scrum Master must write the architectural document while Developers continue coding.

questions.explanation: Scrum relies on empirical process control. Architecture emerges iteratively as valuable, usable Increments are built, inspected, and adapted.

recommendation.topic: Scrum Events (Sprint, Planning, Daily Scrum, Review, Retrospective)
recommendation.action: Practice high-impact event facilitation techniques that keep events strictly within their maximum timeboxes.

questions.question: [Scenario 5] [Scrum Artifacts & Commitments] During a Daily Scrum, a Developer hesitates to mention that a blocking dependency will delay their work by 3 days because they fear criticism from management. Which Scrum values are lacking in the team culture? (Context variation 1.5)

options.text: Openness
Courage
Command Authority
Predictive Control

questions.explanation: Openness and Courage are essential Scrum values. Team members need courage to speak up about impediments, and openness to collaborate transparently without fear.

questions.question: [Scenario 101] [Scrum Theory & Empiricism] An enterprise product organization assigns three separate Product Owners to a single Scrum Team, with each Product Owner directing different feature sets. options.text: The Developers must automatically accept all mid-Sprint additions requested by the Product Owner.

Scope can be negotiated between Product Owner and Developers as long as the change does not endanger the Sprint Goal or compromise quality.
Developers should secretly fix the bug without informing the Product Owner or documenting it in the Sprint Backlog.

questions.explanation: In Scrum, scope may be clarified and re-negotiated between the Product Owner and Developers as more is learned, provided the change does not endanger the Sprint Goal.

options.text: Release the code, because Product Owner approval overrides the Definition of Done.

Change the Definition of Done retroactively to exclude regression testing.
